It was notable for its economic development and maritime trade, particularly with the Byzantine Empire and Eastern Mediterranean, although somewhat confined by Venetian supremacy on the sea. Ancona was an oligarchic republic ruled by six Elders, who were elected by the three terzieri into which the city was divided: S. Pietro, Porto, and Capodimonte. The rule of the Jagiellonian dynasty in Poland between 1385 and 1572 spans the Late Middle Ages and the Early Modern Period in European history. The Lithuanian Grand Duke Jogaila (Władysław II Jagiełło) founded the dynasty; his marriage to Queen Jadwiga of Poland in 1386 strengthened an ongoing Polish–Lithuanian union. The partnership brought vast territories controlled by the Grand Duchy of Lithuania into Poland's sphere of influence and proved beneficial for both the Polish and Lithuanian people, who coexisted and cooperated in one of the largest political entities in Europe for the next four centuries.
In the Baltic Sea region, Poland engaged in an ongoing conflict with the Teutonic Knights. The struggles led to a major battle, the Battle of Grunwald of 1410, but there was also the milestone Peace of Thorn of 1466 under King Casimir IV Jagiellon; the treaty defined the basis of the future Duchy of Prussia. In the south, Poland confronted the Ottoman Empire and the Crimean Tatars, and in the east, Poles helped Lithuania fight the Grand Duchy of Moscow. Poland's and Lithuania's territorial expansion included the far north region of Livonia.
In the Jagiellonian period, Poland developed as a feudal state with a predominantly agricultural economy and an increasingly dominant landed nobility. The Nihil novi act adopted by the Polish Sejm in 1505 transferred most of the legislative power in the state from the monarch to the Sejm.

It expressed the idea of the kingdom as a permanent political entity, distinct from the person of its reigning monarch and possessing its own rights, institutions, and territories.
The concept emerged during the consolidation of the Polish monarchy under the last Piast kings and acquired particular importance under the Angevin dynasty. It increasingly came to signify the continuity and indivisibility of the kingdom, whose lands and rights could not be freely disposed of by the monarch as personal or dynastic property. The Crown also provided a framework for claims to territories formerly associated with the Polish kingdom but lying outside its contemporary borders.
From the late 14th century, the Crown played an important role in the development of the Polish political community and in relations with the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. Over time, the term also acquired a territorial and institutional meaning, referring to the lands and institutions of the Kingdom of Poland. Following the Union of Lublin in 1569, it commonly designated the Polish constituent part of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, distinguished from the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.
